procedural_history.originating_court: Gram Cutcherry of Bankat, district of Champaran
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated July 20, 1954, of the Patna High Court in Criminal Miscellaneous No. 228 of 1954, which summarily dismissed an application under Arts. 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Uma Shankar Prasad instituted a case in the Gram Cutcherry against eight persons, including Baldeo Singh, Ramdeo Singh, and Sheodhar Singh, for allegedly forcibly cutting and removing crops. The Gram Cutcherry acquitted all the accused. Uma Shankar Prasad then appealed to the High Court under s. 67 of the Act. The High Court summarily dismissed the appeal.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The three accused, Baldeo Singh, Ramdeo Singh, and Sheodhar Singh, appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave from the High Court's order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal for Ramdeo Singh and Sheodhar Singh, setting aside their conviction and sentence. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction of Bakko Singh but reduced his sentence to a fine.

decision.conviction_status: Set aside for Ramdeo Singh and Sheodhar Singh; Upheld for Bakko Singh
decision.sentence_status: Set aside for Ramdeo Singh and Sheodhar Singh; Reduced for Bakko Singh to a fine of Rs. 30/-
directions: Ramdeo Singh and Sheodhar Singh to be discharged from bail.

issue.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of the ordinary criminal courts to try the case was barred by the provisions of the Act, particularly Section 68, which grants jurisdiction to the Gram Cutcherry.

law.text: Grants a Gram Cutcherry jurisdiction "concurrent with that of the Criminal Court" but explicitly states this is "subject to the provisions of this Act."

States that "No court shall take cognizance of any case or suit which is cognizable under the Act by a bench of the Gram Cutcherry" unless a contrary order is passed by a Sub-Divisional Magistrate or Munsif.
Provide the mechanism for a Sub-Divisional Magistrate or Munsif to withdraw a case from a Gram Cutcherry and transfer it to an ordinary court, particularly to prevent a miscarriage of justice.

application.text: The Court analyzed the appellant's argument that Section 62 created a system of concurrent jurisdiction, which was discriminatory because it allowed a party to choose between the ordinary courts and the Gram Cutcherry, each with substantially different procedures.

The Court rejected this interpretation by reading Section 62 in conjunction with Section 68. It emphasized that Section 62 is explicitly "subject to the provisions of this Act," which includes Section 68.

The Court found that Section 68 acts as a clear bar on the jurisdiction of ordinary courts. It establishes the general rule that a case cognizable by a Gram Cutcherry must be tried there, and no other court can take it up initially.

The Court explained that the phrase "concurrent jurisdiction" in Section 62 does not give the complainant a choice of forum. Instead, its purpose is to ensure that if a case is later transferred out of the Gram Cutcherry by a higher authority (under Sections 70 or 73), the ordinary criminal courts will have the jurisdiction to hear it.
Therefore, the overall scheme of the Act is that the Gram Cutcherry has primary and exclusive jurisdiction, save for exceptional cases where a Sub-Divisional Magistrate or Munsif intervenes.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the jurisdiction of the ordinary criminal courts was indeed barred by Section 68 of the Act. The Court held that cases cognizable by a Gram Cutcherry must be tried by it, and the reference to "concurrent jurisdiction" in Section 62 only applies in exceptional circumstances, such as when a case is transferred from the Gram Cutcherry by a higher judicial authority. This interpretation means there is no choice of forum for the parties, and thus no discrimination.

issue.issue_text: Whether the procedural requirements under rules 60 and 61 of the Act were violated.

facts: The appellants' counsel argued that rules 60 and 61 of the Bihar Gram Cutcherry Rules, 1949, had been violated.
law: Rule 60(2) requires that the decision of the full bench must be signed by its members.
The rule also requires that if a dissenting judgment is delivered, the minute of dissent must be recorded under the signatures of the dissenting members.
application: The Court found that these specific requirements were fulfilled in the present case.
The Court noted that the appellants had not presented any materials or evidence that would lead to the conclusion that the rules had been violated.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that rules 60 and 61 were not violated and rejected the appellants' argument on this issue.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of the ordinary criminal courts to try the case was barred by the provisions of the Act, particularly Section 68, which grants jurisdiction to the Gram Cutcherry.
appellant_arguments: Section 62 of the Act provides for concurrent jurisdiction, which leaves it open for a party to choose between the ordinary criminal courts and a Gram Cutcherry.
Allowing this choice leads to discrimination, as the procedure in ordinary criminal courts is substantially different from the one followed by a Gram Cutcherry.
respondent_arguments: Section 68 of the Act acts as a bar, stating that no court shall take cognizance of a case cognizable by a Gram Cutcherry unless a specific order is passed to the contrary.

The reference to 'concurrent jurisdiction' in Section 62 is explainable by other provisions (Sections 69, 70, and 73) which allow for the transfer or withdrawal of cases. It ensures that ordinary courts can hear a case if it is transferred to them, not that a complainant has an initial choice of forum.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the procedural requirements under rules 60 and 61 of the Act were violated.
appellant_arguments: The procedural requirements under rules 60 and 61 of the Act were violated.
respondent_arguments: The procedural requirements were fulfilled, and the appellants failed to provide any materials or evidence to show that the rules had been violated.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A statutory provision that appears to grant concurrent jurisdiction to a special tribunal and an ordinary court is not unconstitutionally discriminatory if another provision in the same statute bars the ordinary court from taking cognizance of any case that is cognizable by the special tribunal. In such a scheme, the jurisdiction of the special tribunal is exclusive, unless a case is specifically transferred from it under other provisions of the statute.
obiter: A conviction is manifestly erroneous and cannot be sustained when there is no legal evidence on the record to support it.
In an appeal, the Supreme Court can exercise the same power of superintendence under Article 227 of the Constitution as the High Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: On a proper construction of the Act, there is no discrimination because Section 62, which grants concurrent jurisdiction, is expressly subject to the other provisions of the Act, including Section 68. Section 68 mandates that no court shall take cognizance of a case cognizable by a Gram Cutcherry unless a specific order to the contrary is passed. Therefore, a case cognizable by a Gram Cutcherry must be tried there, removing any choice for the complainant and thus negating the claim of discrimination.
legal_tests_applied: Harmonious construction of statutory provisions, where one section (s. 62) is read as being 'subject to' another, overriding section (s. 68).
Analysis of the 'whole scheme' of a legislative chapter to determine the intended jurisdiction and procedure.
The principle that a party alleging a procedural violation bears the burden of placing materials before the court to prove that violation.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's discrimination argument failed because it did not take into account the other provisions of the Act; specifically, it ignored that Section 62 is expressly subject to Section 68, which removes the choice of forum that was the basis of the discrimination claim.

Regarding the procedural violation claim, the appellants failed to provide any evidence, as the court noted that 'no materials have been placed before us which may lead to the conclusion that rr. 60 and 61 have been violated.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent's interpretation of the Act's jurisdictional scheme was accepted. The court agreed that Section 68 acts as a bar to ordinary courts and that the 'reference to concurrent jurisdiction in s. 62 is explainable by reason of the provisions in ss. 69, 70 and 73, so that on the transfer or withdrawal of a case from the Gram Cutcberry... it may not be said that the ordinary criminal Courts also have no jurisdiction to try it.'

On the procedural issue, the respondent's position prevailed because the court found that the procedural 'requirements were fulfilled in the present case' and the appellants offered no evidence to the contrary.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning upholds the legislative scheme of the Act, which intends for cases cognizable by a Gram Cutcherry to be tried by that body, 'save in those exceptional cases which are provided for in ss. 70 and 73,' thereby preserving the specialized forum created by the legislature.
